passages.title: Leo's New Trick
sentences: Leo wanted to land a kickflip.
He tried ten times at the skate park.
He fell off each time.
He sat on the ramp and frowned.
Then he got up and tried again.
This time, his feet came down on the board.
He rolled all the way to the end.
Leo threw his arms up and grinned.
"I did it!" he yelled.

passages.title: The Rock Club
sentences: On Tuesday, Maya went to the new rock club at the library.
All the other kids were new to her.
They sat in pairs and talked and laughed.
Maya sat at the end of the long table by herself.
She looked down at her rock and turned it in her hands.
The room was full of kids, but Maya felt alone.
Then a girl with a robot pin sat down next to her.
It was Priya.
"Is that quartz?" Priya asked.
Maya looked up and smiled.
"Yes," she said. "I found it by the creek."

passages.title: Earth from Space
sentences: Astronauts live and work on a space station high above Earth.
The station goes all the way around Earth in about ninety minutes.
From a big window, they can see the whole curve of the planet.
They see blue oceans, white clouds and brown sand.
At night, they see the lights of cities as tiny dots.
Many astronauts say they stare out the window for a long time.
They say Earth looks small and lovely at the same time.
They feel amazed.
This big, quiet, amazed feeling has a name.
It is called wonder.

passages.title: Storm Night
sentences: Sam was staying the night at Grandma Rose's house above the bakery.
After dinner, dark clouds came in from the sea.
Soon, rain hit the windows hard.
A flash of light filled the room, and then thunder boomed.
Pixel ran under the bed and shook.
Sam's heart beat fast.
He pulled the blanket up to his chin.
Grandma Rose came in and sat on the end of the bed.
"Storms are loud, but this house is strong and safe," she said.
"Let's count from the flash to the boom."
At the next flash, they counted to five before the boom.
Each time, the count got longer.
"That means the storm is moving away," said Grandma Rose.
Sam took slow breaths.
His hands felt warm and still.
Pixel came out and curled up by his feet.
Soon the only sound was soft rain, and Sam fell asleep.

passages.title: The Last Match
sentences: On Saturday, the Harbor Town Gulls played the last soccer match of the year.
Ana and Ben were both on the team.
The score was one to one, with two minutes left.
Ben passed the ball to Ana.
Ana ran past two players and kicked the ball as hard as she could.
It flew into the top corner of the net.
The whistle blew, and the Gulls had won.
Ana jumped up and down, and the whole team ran to hug her.
On the bus ride home, Ana smiled at the window.
At dinner, she told the story of the goal three times.
That night, she put her muddy ball on the shelf next to her bed.

passages.title: The Spring Concert
sentences: On Friday night, the Harbor Middle School band played its spring concert.
Ana had a short trumpet solo in the very last song.
She had practiced it every day after school for a whole month.
Before the show, her hands felt cold, and she kept checking her sheet music.
Then the lights went down, and the band began to play.
When her solo came, Ana stood up and lifted her trumpet.
The first note came out clear and strong.
She played every note exactly the way she had practiced it.
When she sat down, the whole audience clapped, and Ben whistled from the third row.
After the concert, Ana held her trumpet case tight and smiled at everyone she passed.
"I played the whole solo without one mistake," she told her mom.
On the drive home, she hummed the tune of her solo again and again.

passages.title: Dolphins by the Ferry
sentences: On Sunday morning, Sam and Maya took the ferry to Gull Island.
Maya sat by the rail with her sketchbook open on her knees.
Halfway across the bay, she saw a gray fin rise out of the water.
Then she saw another fin, and then five more.
A group of dolphins was swimming right beside the ferry.
They leaped out of the waves in smooth curves and slid back into the sea.
Maya put down her pencil and stood very still.
Her mouth opened, but she did not say a word.
She watched the dolphins until they turned and swam out of sight.
Then she turned to Sam and asked question after question.
"How do they swim so fast? Do they ever sleep? Where are they going?"
Sam did not know the answers, so they planned to find a book about dolphins at the library.
That night, Maya drew the dolphins across a whole page of her sketchbook.

passages.title: The Fox and the Crow
sentences: One morning, a crow spotted a piece of cheese on a windowsill outside a farmhouse kitchen.
She snatched it in her beak and flew up to the highest branch of a tall oak tree.
There she settled comfortably, very pleased with herself, to enjoy her delicious breakfast in peace.
A hungry fox was trotting along the path below, and he noticed the cheese at once.
He sat down beneath the tree and gazed up at the crow with a friendly, admiring smile.
"Good morning, beautiful bird," he called.
"Your feathers shine in the sunlight, and your eyes are bright and clever."
"A bird so lovely must have a lovely voice as well."
"If you would sing just one song for me, I would call you the queen of all the birds."
The crow puffed out her chest and lifted her head high.
Nobody had ever praised her like this before, and she wanted the fox to hear her voice.
She opened her beak wide and gave the loudest caw she could.
At that very moment, the cheese slipped out of her beak and tumbled down to the ground.
The fox snapped it up and gulped it down in one bite.
"Thank you for breakfast," said the fox, licking his whiskers.
"In return, here is some advice: be careful of anyone who praises you only to get something from you."
Then he trotted away down the path.
The crow sat on her branch with an empty beak, and her feathers drooped.
She wished, more than anything, that she had kept her beak shut.

credit.title: The Fox and the Crow
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Night Train
sentences: Sam had wanted to ride a sleeper train for years, and in July he finally got his chance.
He and Grandma Rose were taking the overnight train to visit his uncle in a city far to the north.
The night before, Sam spread his paper map across the kitchen table and traced the route with a green pen.
He counted eleven stations between Harbor Town and the city.
At the station, he read every line on the departure board twice, and he could not keep his feet still.
Their sleeping compartment was tiny, with two narrow beds, one above the other.
For the first few hours, Sam sat by the window and checked off each station on his map.
Then the sky grew dark, and Grandma Rose fell asleep in the lower bed.
Sam climbed into the top bed, but he could not fall asleep.
The train rocked and clicked, and the little room felt strange and much too quiet.
He thought about Pixel curled up at the end of his own bed, far away at home.
He wished that someone were awake to talk to.
Near dawn, a soft gray light came in around the edges of the blind, and Sam lifted it.
The train was crossing a high bridge over a wide valley.
Far below, a river curved between dark green hills, and mist floated above the water.
In the distance, the snowy tops of the mountains were turning pink in the first sunlight.
Sam held his breath and did not move until the bridge was behind them.
Then he found the river on his map and marked the bridge with a small star.
When Grandma Rose woke up, he showed her the star and said, "That was the best part of the whole trip."

passages.title: The Bone in the Hill
sentences: Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils, the remains of plants and animals that lived long ago.
Many of them spend their summers in badlands, which are areas of dry, rocky hills with very few plants.
In the badlands, wind and rain slowly wear away the rock, and ancient bones are sometimes uncovered at the surface.
One paleontologist searches the same badlands for six weeks every summer.
Most days, she walks for hours with her eyes on the ground and finds nothing but broken stones and dust.
One hot afternoon, late in her third week, she noticed a dark brown shape poking out of a gray slope.
It had a smooth, curved surface, and its color was different from the rocks around it.
She knelt down and brushed away the dust with her fingers.
Her heart began to pound, because she recognized what it was: the rounded end of a very large bone.
Over the next ten days, her team uncovered the bone slowly, using small picks, dental tools and soft brushes.
They could not hurry, because a fossil can crack if it is handled roughly.
Over many hours, a thigh bone longer than a grown person's leg appeared from the rock.
The team believed it came from a large plant-eating dinosaur that lived about seventy million years ago.
To protect it for the journey, they wrapped it in strips of cloth dipped in wet plaster, much like a cast for a broken arm.
On the last day, the team lifted the heavy plaster jacket into the back of a truck.
Before she left, the paleontologist sat on the slope and looked out over the silent hills.
No person had ever seen that bone before her team found it.
For millions of years, it had lain hidden under the ground, and soon it would rest in a museum where thousands of visitors could see it.
She smiled, wiped the dust from her hands and wrote the date in her field notebook.
Years later, she still told her students that touching that bone was the best moment of her career.

passages.title: Waiting for the Rover
sentences: After a journey of about seven months through space, a rover was finally about to land on Mars.
The rover was a robot about the size of a small car, with six wheels, many cameras and a long arm for studying rocks.
Hundreds of engineers had spent years designing and building it.
One of them had worked on its wheels for five years, testing them again and again on sand and sharp stones.
Landing on Mars is very difficult, because the rover arrives many times faster than a jet plane.
In about seven minutes, it must slow down almost to a stop, using a heat shield, a huge parachute and small rockets.
Nobody on Earth can steer it during those minutes.
On landing day, a radio signal from Mars took more than ten minutes to reach Earth.
So by the time the team heard that the landing had begun, it was already over, and all they could do was wait for the news.
In the control room, the wheel engineer sat at his desk and stared at the screens.
His hands were cold, and he kept tapping his foot on the floor.
A voice read out each message as it arrived: the heat shield, the parachute, the rockets.
Then came the words the whole room had been waiting for: "Touchdown confirmed."
The room filled with cheers, and the engineer jumped up and hugged the people next to him.
He laughed, and at the same time his eyes filled with tears.
A few minutes later, the first picture from the rover appeared on the big screen.
It was grainy and black and white, and it showed only dusty ground and a few small rocks.
To the team, it looked more beautiful than any picture they had ever seen.
The engineer leaned close to the screen and thought about the six wheels he had helped to build, now resting on the ground of another planet.

items.prompt: How did Leo feel at the end?

items.explain: Leo felt proud. He threw his arms up, grinned and yelled "I did it!" in the last two sentences.

items.prompt: Maya sat at the end of the table by herself. Which word names her feeling?
items.hint: Find the sentence that says how Maya felt in the full room. Then pick the word that means the same.
items.explain: Maya felt lonely. The story says the room was full of kids, but Maya felt alone. Feeling alone is called lonely.

items.hint: Find the part after Priya sits down. Look for what Maya does with her face.
items.explain: "Maya looked up and smiled." She smiled after Priya sat down and asked about her rock.

items.hint: Read the last three sentences. The text gives the feeling a name.
items.explain: They feel wonder. The last sentences say the astronauts feel amazed, and this big, quiet, amazed feeling is called wonder.

items.explain: One good answer is: If I saw Earth from space, I would feel wonder because I could see the whole planet. Any honest answer is fine.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences. Does each one show a scared feeling or a calm feeling?

cards.text: Pixel ran under the bed and shook.
He pulled the blanket up to his chin.
His hands felt warm and still.
Pixel curled up by his feet.

items.hint: Fast and shaking bodies often mean scared. Slow and still bodies often mean calm.
items.explain: Scared: Pixel shook, Sam's heart beat fast, and Sam pulled up the blanket. Calm: slow breaths, warm and still hands, and Pixel curled up. The calm parts come after Grandma Rose helps them count.

items.explain: Ana felt joyful. She smiled at the window on the bus, and she told the story of the goal three times at dinner.

items.explain: Maya asked Sam question after question: "How do they swim so fast? Do they ever sleep? Where are they going?" Asking questions shows she was curious.

items.prompt: The fox praised the crow, and she puffed out her chest. Which word best names her feeling at that moment?
items.hint: Read the two sentences right after the fox stops talking. Look at what the crow does with her body, and why.
items.explain: The crow felt proud. Right after the fox praised her, she puffed out her chest and lifted her head high. Nobody had ever praised her like this before.

items.prompt: How did the crow feel at the end of the fable?
items.hint: Her feeling changes during the fable. Read only the last two sentences, and look at her feathers and her wish.
items.explain: The crow felt embarrassed. At the end, her feathers drooped, and she wished she had kept her beak shut. She felt silly for believing the fox. She was proud in the middle of the fable, not at the end.

items.hint: Read the paragraph about the bridge. Is Sam quick and busy, or quiet and still? Then look at what he is looking at.
items.explain: Sam felt wonder. He was looking at a river, mist and pink mountain tops, and he held his breath and did not move. His excitement came earlier, at the station, and his loneliness came in the dark night.

items.hint: A pounding heart can go with more than one feeling. Read the whole sentence, and think about how long she had been searching.
items.explain: She felt excited. Her heart pounded because she recognized a very large bone after almost three weeks of finding nothing. A fast heart can also mean afraid, but nothing in this account is dangerous.

items.prompt: This account mixes facts and feelings. Sort each sentence: does it show a feeling, or does it only tell a fact?

cards.text: She smiled and wrote the date in her field notebook.
Touching that bone was the best moment of her career.

A fossil can crack if it is handled roughly.
The dinosaur lived about seventy million years ago.

items.hint: For each sentence, ask: does it tell what the paleontologist felt inside, or something that would be true for anyone?
items.explain: Feelings: her heart pounded, she smiled, and she called it the best moment of her career. Facts: wind and rain wear away rock, a fossil can crack, and the dinosaur lived about seventy million years ago.

items.explain: He felt nervous, then joyful. While he waited, his hands were cold and he kept tapping his foot. After "Touchdown confirmed," he jumped up, hugged people and laughed.

items.explain: "The engineer leaned close to the screen and thought about the six wheels he had helped to build, now resting on the ground of another planet." He is thinking about his own work, now on Mars. That shows pride.

items.explain: One good answer is: When the rover landed, the engineer felt joyful and relieved. I think so because the long wait was over. Any honest answer is fine.

steps.say: The question asks how Leo felt at the end. So I read the last sentences.
Leo threw his arms up and grinned. He yelled, "I did it!"
Arms up and a big grin show a good feeling.
He did a hard trick after many tries. The good feeling after you do something hard is called proud.
